decisions.reason: The linked roller-lifter part is unscoped and is not proven to be the required AFM lifter for every 5.3L application; publishing it risks the wrong valvetrain hardware.

sourceEvidence.title: Excessive Oil Consumption & AFM Lifter Failure (5.3L V8)
sourceEvidence.howToFix: For oil consumption, GM's TSB remedy involves replacing the AFM oil-pressure relief valve/deflector and often the pistons/rings; many owners delete AFM (range-disabler or PCM tune + delete kit) to prevent recurrence. For a failed lifter, replace the lifters (and cam if scored), commonly done alongside an AFM delete. Eligible owners can file under the Siqueiros settlement.

decisions.reason: The repair is conditional on rust-jacking diagnosis and the failed front side, while this wheel-speed-sensor claim has no location or fitment scope.

sourceEvidence.title: ABS False Activation at Low Speed from Wheel Speed Sensor Corrosion
sourceEvidence.howToFix: Per the GM TSB, remove the front wheel speed sensors, thoroughly clean the corrosion from the sensor mounting surfaces on the steering knuckles, and reinstall (replacing sensors damaged by rust jacking). Severely corroded hub/bearing assemblies with integral reluctor rings must be replaced.

decisions.reason: The catalog could not confirm this wheel-speed-sensor claim for the stated 4.3L application, and the article also allows a hub or EBCM repair instead.

sourceEvidence.title: Kelsey-Hayes ABS: Wheel Speed Sensor / EBCM Faults & Corroded Grounds
sourceEvidence.howToFix: Scan for C-codes and inspect. Clean and tighten the EBCM ground straps at the radiator support first. Replace corroded front wheel-speed sensors / hub bearing assemblies as needed. If the EBCM itself is faulty, a repair-and-return board service is a cost-effective alternative to a new module.

decisions.reason: The article explicitly states that reduced DC charging is an intentional software limitation with no repair; a 12-volt vehicle battery is the wrong role.

sourceEvidence.title: DC Fast Charging Speed Reduction After Battery Recall
sourceEvidence.howToFix: There is currently no fix — the reduced charging speed is an intentional software limitation by GM to protect the replacement battery. Precondition the battery before arriving at a fast charger by setting navigation to a DC fast charge station (the Bolt will warm the battery en route, improving charging speed by 10-20%). Avoid fast charging when the battery is below 20% or above 80% for best charging rates. Some aftermarket tools can monitor BMS temperature limits, but modifying the charging software voids the battery warranty.

decisions.reason: The front hub claim has no persisted engine, side, or application scope and the current catalog run did not confirm it.

sourceEvidence.title: Front Wheel Bearing / Hub Assembly Failure (Humming, ABS Light)
sourceEvidence.howToFix: Confirm the noisy side (noise worsens when weight shifts to the bad bearing during cornering) and check for play. Replace the complete sealed hub/bearing assembly; replacing in pairs is recommended if one side has failed from age. A relearn is not usually needed, but the ABS codes clear once the integrated speed sensor is restored.

decisions.reason: The article requires diagnosis between the high-pressure and in-tank fuel pumps; this unscoped in-tank module would surface without that distinction.

sourceEvidence.title: Fuel Pump / High-Pressure Fuel Pump Failure (Stalling, No-Start, Fuel Starvation)
sourceEvidence.howToFix: Diagnose fuel-rail pressure with a scan tool; low pressure with P0087 indicates a failing HPFP or supply (in-tank) pump or a clogged filter. Replace the failed pump (HPFP is engine-top mounted; the in-tank pump/module requires tank access). Replace the fuel filter at recommended intervals to reduce strain. Track/high-output cars often upgrade the pump and lines to prevent starvation.

decisions.reason: The linked roller-lifter part is not proven to be the required L99 AFM lifter and complete repair hardware, so the unscoped claim remains unsafe.

sourceEvidence.title: L99 AFM Lifter Failure and Camshaft Damage on 6.2L Automatic Cars
sourceEvidence.howToFix: Diagnosis usually starts with a persistent misfire, ticking, and cylinder-specific contribution loss; compression/leakdown and valvetrain inspection help confirm a failed lifter. Proper repair typically involves replacing the failed AFM lifters, trays/guides, and often the camshaft if lobe wear is present; many owners also replace related gaskets, head bolts, and oil pump components while inside. Continued driving can worsen metal contamination and increase repair cost.

decisions.reason: The Dayco DP820 water pump is directly prescribed during Optispark access and was independently reconfirmed for every 1993-1997 Camaro LT1 year.

sourceEvidence.title: LT1 Optispark distributor failure (moisture/oil/coolant intrusion)
sourceEvidence.howToFix: Replace the Optispark distributor (and the optical sensor/cap-and-rotor as an assembly). Because the water pump must be removed to access it, the accepted practice is to replace the water pump at the same time and to install a vented-style Optispark plus a small tube/tee routed into the water pump weep hole to divert coolant away from the distributor. Verify grounds, coil and plug wires first, since those are cheaper and can mimic the symptoms.

decisions.reason: The article prescribes a regulator-with-motor assembly, while Cardone 42-102 is only a window motor.

sourceEvidence.title: Power Window Motor Failure
sourceEvidence.howToFix: Replace window motor and regulator as an assembly. Aftermarket units are affordable and readily available.

decisions.reason: The 1984-only Cross-Fire article directly prescribes the updated coolant-temperature sensor, and NGK EF0008 was confirmed for the complete frozen scope.

sourceEvidence.title: Cross-Fire Injection Driveability Problems (1984 L83)
sourceEvidence.howToFix: Restore the system to spec: replace the coolant temperature sensor (updated weather-pack type) and oil pressure switch, reseal the intake manifold, rebuild or rebush worn throttle bodies, clean or replace injectors, and synchronize the two throttle bodies. Specialist Cross-Fire shops can rebuild the throttle bodies when wear is advanced.

decisions.reason: The article directly prescribes the affected sealed hub assembly, and SKF BR930663 was confirmed across every frozen 2005-2009 Equinox year.

sourceEvidence.title: Front Wheel Bearing and Hub Assembly Failure Triggering ABS/Traction Warnings
sourceEvidence.howToFix: Diagnosis involves road-testing for bearing noise, checking for wheel play, and scanning ABS data for an intermittent or weak wheel speed signal. The standard repair is replacement of the affected hub assembly, often in pairs if both sides are noisy or high-mileage. After replacement, technicians should verify sensor wiring condition and clear any stored ABS codes.

decisions.reason: The 3.4L article directly prescribes head-gasket replacement, and MAHLE 4956 was confirmed for every frozen 2005-2009 application.

sourceEvidence.title: Head Gasket Coolant Leak and Overheating on 3.4L V6
sourceEvidence.howToFix: Diagnosis usually includes pressure-testing the cooling system, checking for combustion gases in the coolant, inspecting for coolant loss with no visible leak, and verifying whether the engine has been overheated. Repair typically involves replacing the head gaskets, checking head flatness, resurfacing if needed, and replacing related components such as intake gaskets, head bolts, thermostat, and coolant. If overheating was severe, the cylinder heads or engine may also need machine work or replacement.

decisions.reason: The article directly prescribes the water pump when the leak is at the weep hole, and Aisin WPGM-604V was confirmed across both stated V6 engine slices.

sourceEvidence.title: Water Pump and Coolant Crossover Pipe Gasket Leaks (3.5L/3.9L)
sourceEvidence.howToFix: Pressure-test the cooling system to pinpoint the source. A weep-hole drip or coolant flung by the belt means the water pump — replace it (and the belt if soaked). Coolant at the rear/right of the engine points to the crossover pipe gaskets — replace both crossover gaskets. Refill with the correct Dex-Cool and bleed the system. Do not keep driving with a suspected bad water pump; overheating these aluminum engines risks head-gasket damage.

decisions.reason: The article directly allows replacement of the intermediate steering shaft, and Cardone 1C-1005S was confirmed for the complete 2004-2007 scope.

sourceEvidence.title: Electric Power Steering Column Clunk and Intermediate Steering Shaft Noise
sourceEvidence.howToFix: Diagnosis involves isolating the noise from suspension components and checking for play or binding in the intermediate shaft. The typical repair is lubricating the shaft if applicable per service procedure or replacing the intermediate steering shaft with an updated part. If noise persists, inspect strut mounts and lower steering column joints to rule out similar sounds.

decisions.reason: The unscoped Aisin thermostat would also surface for engines where catalog evidence says absent and contradicts the article explicit OEM/ACDelco instruction.

sourceEvidence.title: P0128 — Coolant Below Thermostat Regulating Temperature from Thermostat Stuck Open
sourceEvidence.howToFix: Verify coolant level and confirm the ECT sensor reads accurately, then replace the thermostat and gasket (ACDelco 131-158 on the 2.4L). Use an OEM/ACDelco thermostat — cheap aftermarket units frequently fail to regulate and leave the code active. Refill and bleed the cooling system, then confirm the engine reaches full operating temperature.

decisions.reason: The article specifically directs Denso or NTK oxygen sensors; the Bosch claim conflicts with that reviewed supplier requirement.

sourceEvidence.title: Oxygen Sensor Failure
sourceEvidence.howToFix: Replace failed oxygen sensor(s). Use Denso or NTK OEM-quality sensors. Address any oil consumption issue to prevent premature fouling of new sensor.

decisions.reason: The unscoped gasket claim spans Gen III, IV, and V engines and years without proving the correct manifold/gasket application for each branch.

sourceEvidence.title: Broken Exhaust Manifold Bolts on 5.3L/6.2L V8 Causing Exhaust Tick and False P0420
sourceEvidence.howToFix: Inspect the manifold flanges for soot/leak tracks and the corner bolts for breakage. Repair is to extract the broken bolt shanks (often requires drilling/extractor or a slide-hammer style broken-bolt kit), replace the manifold gaskets, and reinstall with upgraded fasteners — ARP 134-1102 header bolts on Gen III/IV LS (4.8/5.3/6.0) or ARP 134-1104 on Gen V LT (5.3 L83 / 6.2 L86) — torqued in sequence with anti-seize. Re-evaluate any P0420 after the leak is sealed before condemning the catalytic converter or O2 sensors.

decisions.reason: The article explicitly calls for the upgraded steel-backed Fel-Pro MS98016T design; the unscoped MAHLE claim does not satisfy that instruction.

sourceEvidence.title: Intake Manifold Gasket Vacuum Leak (Rough Idle, Cold-Start Misfire, Lean Codes)
sourceEvidence.howToFix: Smoke-test the intake to confirm the leak, then replace the intake manifold gasket set with an upgraded steel-backed design (Fel-Pro MS98016T for 4.8/5.3/6.0 is the widely-used set). Because the intake must come off, it's smart to replace the knock sensors and their harness (a separate known failure that also lives under the intake) at the same time. Inspect the PCV and vacuum lines while apart.

decisions.reason: The current regulator assembly has no confirmed catalog application for any reviewed engine slice and does not prove the article specified side/design.

sourceEvidence.title: Power Window Regulator Failure (Window Off-Track or Won't Roll Up)
sourceEvidence.howToFix: Replace the window regulator-with-motor assembly (e.g., Dorman 741-442 front driver side for 2007-2013; OE-fix designs add reinforced cable guides). Inspect the door-jamb wiring harness for broken conductors and test the master switch before assuming the regulator. Lubricate the run channels to reduce load on the new regulator.

decisions.component: Axle Differential Bearing and Seal Kit
decisions.reason: Differential bearing kits depend on axle, ratio, carrier, and drivetrain details that are absent from this public claim, and the catalog run did not confirm it.

sourceEvidence.title: Rear Differential Whine / Pinion Bearing Howl and Seal Leak
sourceEvidence.howToFix: Confirm the source by checking pinion/yoke play and inspecting for a gear-oil leak at the pinion seal and axle seals. Repair requires replacing the pinion and/or carrier bearings and pinion seal and correctly setting bearing preload and gear pattern (special tools required — not a basic DIY). Severe cases need a ring-and-pinion set. Refill with correct spec gear oil and friction modifier for limited-slip axles.

decisions.reason: The oil-in-plug-well issue directly prescribes the valve-cover gasket, and MAHLE VS50656 was confirmed for every stated 2012-2018 1.8L application.

sourceEvidence.title: Ignition Coil and Spark Plug Misfire from Valve Cover Gasket Oil Leak (1.8L)
sourceEvidence.howToFix: Replace worn spark plugs and any failed ignition coil(s). Critically, inspect the spark plug wells for oil - if present, replace the valve cover gasket to eliminate the root cause, otherwise misfires recur.

decisions.reason: The unscoped exhaust-gasket claim crosses multiple LS/LT generations without proving the correct manifold application for every engine and year.

sourceEvidence.title: Broken Exhaust Manifold Bolts (Startup Ticking)
sourceEvidence.howToFix: Replace the broken bolts and manifold gaskets, torquing new hardware to spec. Heads that snapped flush usually require an extractor or weld-a-nut removal; Dorman and similar makers also sell exhaust-manifold repair clamp kits (e.g. Dorman exhaust manifold hardware kit) that bolt into an unused hole and clamp the manifold down without extracting a seized stud. Use updated bolts and new gaskets to prevent recurrence.

decisions.reason: The Bosch fuel-module claim is not confirmed for the 6.0L branch and does not match the article reviewed ACDelco/Delphi/Spectra choices.

sourceEvidence.title: In-Tank Fuel Pump Module Failure (Long Crank / No-Start)
sourceEvidence.howToFix: Confirm with a fuel-pressure gauge on the Schrader port: good pressure should reach ~58-62 PSI within ~2 seconds of key-on and hold. Also check the fuel-pump relay/fuse and inspect the pump connector for heat damage. Fix is a complete fuel pump module (pump + level sender + strainer). OEM: ACDelco MU1613 (GM 19153711), which includes the seal, float and harness; quality aftermarket options include Delphi/Spectra modules (part roughly $150-350). Drop the tank, replace the module and strainer, and blow out/inspect the tank if rust is present.

decisions.reason: The unscoped DP990 pump conflicts with the reviewed proposal evidence, which limits that pump to earlier applications and uses different 2014+ parts.

sourceEvidence.title: Water Pump Failure / Coolant Leak
sourceEvidence.howToFix: Replace the water pump with an OE-quality unit (ACDelco / GM Genuine or Aisin/Gates equivalent) and fresh dexos-approved coolant; inspect the belt, tensioner and thermostat while there. Avoid the cheapest pumps — some last only ~30k miles versus 100k+ for a quality unit. Pressure-test the system afterward to confirm no residual leaks.

decisions.reason: The 2.2L OHV article directly prescribes the head gasket, and MAHLE 5871G was confirmed across every frozen 1990-1996 application.

sourceEvidence.title: 2.2L OHV Head Gasket Failure
sourceEvidence.howToFix: Replace the head gasket and have the cylinder head checked for warpage — machine the head if out of specification (max 0.003" deviation). Replace the thermostat and inspect the water pump while accessible. Use a quality multi-layer steel gasket and torque head bolts in sequence. Perform a cooling system pressure test after repair.

decisions.reason: The crank-sensor claim has no engine/application scope across seven model years, so catalog confirmation is insufficient for safe public fitment.

sourceEvidence.title: Crankshaft Position Sensor Failure Causing Stalling
sourceEvidence.howToFix: Replace the crankshaft position sensor. The harmonic balancer must be removed for access. Inspect the balancer for rubber separation while it is removed. Use a quality OEM-equivalent sensor. Apply anti-seize to the sensor bolt threads. Clear any stored DTCs after installation.

decisions.reason: The unscoped WPK-818 claim would show to both 1.4T and 1.8L cars although the reviewed fitment proposals use engine-specific water-pump parts.

sourceEvidence.title: Premature Water Pump Failure and Coolant Leaks
sourceEvidence.howToFix: Replace the water pump at the first sign of leaking. On the 1.4T, the water pump is internal and driven by the timing chain, making replacement more labor-intensive ($400-$800). On the 1.8L, it is belt-driven and easier to access ($200-$400). Monitor coolant levels regularly. Replace the thermostat at the same time.

decisions.reason: The cabin-filter part was not confirmed by the catalog for the reviewed Spark application, so its legacy verified flag is insufficient.

sourceEvidence.title: Weak A/C Performance in Hot Weather
sourceEvidence.howToFix: Verify refrigerant charge is at the correct level (do not overcharge). Replace the cabin air filter. Ensure the condenser is clean and free of debris. Aftermarket solutions include adding a condenser fan or upgrading to a slightly larger condenser. Using recirculate mode instead of fresh air helps significantly.
